name: Dho Tarap
tagline: A high farming valley at the heart of Lower Dolpo
meta_description: Dho Tarap in Lower Dolpo at ≈ 4,040 m: Bon and Buddhist gompas, barley at the limit of farming, the Tarap Khola gorge and the high passes to Phoksundo.
summary: Dho Tarap is the main village of the Tarap valley in Lower Dolpo, at about 4,040 m, among the highest farming communities in Nepal. Its stone houses, chortens and Bon and Buddhist gompas sit in a wide, bare valley reached by a 5–6 day trek from Juphal, and linked to Phoksundo Lake by two passes above 5,000 m.
intro: After days of walking up the narrow, roaring gorge of the Tarap Khola, the valley suddenly opens. Dho Tarap spreads across a wide, treeless basin at around 4,000 m: low stone houses with flat roofs, long mani walls, painted chortens, and walled fields of barley that turn green in July and gold in September. Herds of yaks and goats move across the slopes, and snowy ridges close the horizon on every side.

The Tarap valley is one of the four historic valleys of Dolpo, alongside Tsharka, Panzang and Nangkhong. Its name is usually translated as 'auspicious excellent'. Dho, the main village, and its neighbours Lang and Tokyu are together known as Dho Tarap, home to around 900 people at the 2011 census. Both Bon and Tibetan Buddhist traditions are practised here, and the valley's gompas are among the oldest in Dolpo. It is a valley of great age.

Dho Tarap is the high point of the Lower Dolpo circuit, a 12–14 day trek from Juphal through the Tarap Khola gorge to Dho, then over the Numa La and Baga La passes to Phoksundo Lake and back. It is remote, hard and deeply rewarding, with very few other trekkers. We spend two nights in the valley, giving time to acclimatise before the passes and to visit the gompas and families of Dho.

story.title: Farming nomads at the edge of the possible
paras: Agriculture in Dolpo is possible up to about 3,800 to 4,180 m, and the Tarap valley sits right at that limit. Short summers are just long enough to ripen barley, buckwheat and a few vegetables, watered by channels from the streams. The people combine farming with herding in a way known as samadrok, roughly 'farming nomads': in summer, families move their yaks, sheep and goats up to pastures at 4,000 to 5,000 m, returning to the village for harvest and winter.

For centuries the Dolpo-pa relied on trade to survive. Caravans of yaks carried salt from the lakes of the Tibetan plateau south through the high passes, to exchange for grain in the lower hills. This is the life shown in Eric Valli's 1999 film Himalaya, filmed in Dolpo with local people as its cast. After 1959 the border was tightened, Indian salt arrived in the lowlands and the old trade declined, though some caravans still travel north to Tibet each year.

Religion has always been central. Tarap has both Bon and Buddhist gompas, some centuries old, and the mani walls and chortens along the trails are kept in repair by villagers. In 1975 Dho became a village development committee, and in 2017 part of Dolpo Buddha rural municipality. Schools, solar panels and phones have reached the valley, and some young people now study in Kathmandu, but the cycle of planting, herding and festivals still sets the rhythm of the year. The valley endures.

people: Dho Tarap's people are Dolpo-pa, who call themselves Dhol-wa in their own dialect of Tibetan and also speak Nepali. They follow Bon and Tibetan Buddhism, farm barley and buckwheat in short summers, herd yaks, sheep and goats on high pastures, and trade with Tibet and the lower valleys. Amchi, traditional doctors, still serve the valley. In winter some families move south with their animals.

untold.fact: Dho, Lang and Tokyu are the three villages collectively known as Dho Tarap, wards 1–3 of Dolpo Buddha rural municipality. Dho Tarap had 923 people in 205 households at the 2011 census.

Dolpo was historically divided into four valleys: Tsharka ('good growing-place'), Tarap ('auspicious excellent'), Panzang ('abode of monks') and Nangkhong ('innermost place'). Each became a village development committee in 1975.
In Dolpo, farming reaches about 3,800–4,180 m, and the people combine fields with herding on pastures at 4,000–5,000 m in a way of life called samadrok, roughly 'farming nomads'.

taste.name: Dri curd and tsampa
taste.text: In summer, families in Dho Tarap make thick curd from the milk of dri, female yaks, and eat it with tsampa, roasted barley flour, often with a little sugar. If you are offered a bowl in a family kitchen, accept; it is filling, fresh and very local.

highlights.title: The Tarap valley opening
highlights.text: After days in the deep Tarap Khola gorge, the moment the valley opens into a wide, bare basin of fields, chortens and stone villages is one of the best in Dolpo. Arrive in the afternoon light and stop to take it in.

highlights.title: Gompas of two faiths
highlights.text: Dho Tarap has both Bon and Buddhist gompas, some centuries old, with statues, paintings and texts kept by caretakers and lamas. Visiting both shows how the two traditions sit side by side. Go with your guide to find the keyholders.

highlights.title: Mani walls and chortens
highlights.text: Long mani walls and painted chortens line the paths between Dho, Lang and Tokyu. Remember the direction: clockwise around Buddhist ones, counter-clockwise around Bon ones. Your guide will tell you which is which. It matters to local people.

highlights.title: Herding life
highlights.text: In summer, families take yaks, sheep and goats to pastures high above the valley, living in tents or stone huts. With your guide, you may visit a herding camp, see milking and butter-making, and share tea with the herders.

highlights.title: The passes to Phoksundo
highlights.text: From Dho Tarap, the Lower Dolpo circuit crosses the Numa La and the Baga La, both above 5,000 m, over two days to Phoksundo Lake. The views of Dhaulagiri and the Dolpo ranges from the passes are the reward.

how_to_reach.text: From Juphal, trek 5–6 days via Dunai and the Tarap Khola gorge, through Laisicap, Khanigaon and Tarakot, then up the narrowing valley to Dho Tarap. From Phoksundo, cross the Baga La and Numa La passes in 3–4 days. Both routes are remote and need a full trekking crew.

Fly Kathmandu–Nepalgunj (about 1 hour), overnight, then an early flight to Juphal (about 45 minutes). Flights are weather-dependent and frequently delayed. Helicopter charters to Dho Tarap are possible but costly and bring you to 4,000 m too fast.

where_to_stay: Dho Tarap has a few very basic lodges and homestays run by local families, with simple rooms, shared toilets and a warm kitchen. Most organised treks in Lower Dolpo camp, with tents, a cook and porters or mules, which gives flexibility on the route and over the passes. We use campsites on the edge of Dho with a view over the valley, and arrange visits to family kitchens. There are no hotels of any higher standard. Bring a four-season sleeping bag and expect nights well below freezing.
tips: Spend at least two nights at Dho Tarap before crossing the Numa La and Baga La; the passes are above 5,000 m.
Check whether each gompa or chorten is Bon or Buddhist before walking around it; the direction differs.
Bring all cash for the trek in Nepali rupees; there are no ATMs anywhere in the valley.
Keep spare days for weather on the passes and on flights between Juphal and Nepalgunj.
Ask before photographing people, herders and their animals; many families are not used to visitors.

experiences.title: Bon and Buddhist gompas of the Tarap valley
experiences.summary: Spend a morning visiting the gompas of Dho Tarap, some Bon and some Tibetan Buddhist, with a guide who finds the lamas and caretakers and explains how two traditions with different directions of prayer share one high valley.
body: Religious life in Dho Tarap follows both Bon and Tibetan Buddhism. The valley's gompas stand among the fields and on the slopes above the villages, built of stone and mud, painted white and red, with prayer flags snapping in the wind. Some are centuries old and hold statues, wall paintings and texts kept with great care by caretakers and lamas, many of whom also farm and herd. Each has its own history and patrons.

Your guide finds the keyholder for each gompa and explains what you see. In the Buddhist temples, images of the Buddha, Guru Rinpoche and protector deities sit behind butter lamps; in the Bon temples, Tonpa Shenrab and Bon deities, with the yungdrung, the Bon swastika, turning the other way. You walk clockwise around the Buddhist shrines and counter-clockwise around the Bon ones, following local practice. It is easy to get wrong, and villagers appreciate the effort.

The visits are slow and quiet. Sit a while in the assembly halls, ask questions through your guide, and leave a donation at each, NPR 300–500 per person is appropriate. Ask before photographing inside; some lamas allow it without flash, others do not. Between gompas, the walk along mani walls and chortens across the valley is itself part of the experience. Take your time; there is no rush in Tarap.

faqs.q: Is Dho Tarap Bon or Buddhist?
faqs.a: Both. The Tarap valley has Bon and Tibetan Buddhist gompas and families who follow each tradition, living side by side. The two share many practices but differ in founders, texts and lineages, and in the direction they walk around holy places: clockwise for Buddhists, counter-clockwise for Bon. Your guide will tell you which is which.

faqs.q: Can I visit the monasteries in Dho Tarap?
faqs.a: Yes, if you are respectful. Most gompas are kept locked and opened by a caretaker or lama, so go with your guide. Remove shoes and hats, walk in the right direction, do not touch statues and ask before photographing. A donation of NPR 300–500 per person at each gompa is appropriate.

faqs.q: Are there festivals in Dho Tarap?
faqs.a: Yes, the gompas of the Tarap valley hold religious festivals and rituals during the year, often in summer and autumn, with masked dances in some years. Dates follow the Tibetan lunar calendar and change each year. Ask your trekking company to check current dates before you travel if you want to plan around one.

experiences.title: Up the Tarap Khola gorge to Dho
experiences.summary: The approach to Dho Tarap from Juphal: five to six days up the Thuli Bheri and then the deep, narrow gorge of the Tarap Khola, on trails cut into cliffs and over wooden bridges, climbing from forest to bare high valley.
body: From Juphal we walk down to Dunai, the district headquarters on the Thuli Bheri, and follow that river east for a day or two through villages such as Tarakot, an old fortified settlement on a hill above the river. Then the trail turns north into the Tarap Khola, and the valley quickly narrows into a deep gorge. Pine and juniper forest cling to the slopes, and the river roars below.

For two or three days the trail threads through the gorge, sometimes on paths built out from the cliff on stone and wood, sometimes crossing the river on log bridges or small suspension bridges. Camps are in clearings by the river, sheltered by the trees while they last. This is wild, empty country; you may meet only herders and occasional mule trains carrying supplies up to Dho. Days settle into a steady rhythm of walking, tea and camp.

Gradually the trees thin and disappear, the valley widens, and the air turns dry and thin. On the last day you climb into the open upper valley and see the stone villages of Dho Tarap ahead, at about 4,040 m. The steady gain over six days is good for acclimatisation. Trails in the gorge can be damaged by rockfall or floods; check current status before you travel. Few arrivals in Nepal feel as well earned.

faqs.q: How many days does it take to trek to Dho Tarap?
faqs.a: From Juphal airport, it usually takes 5–6 days to reach Dho Tarap via Dunai, Tarakot and the Tarap Khola gorge, walking 5–7 hours a day. The full Lower Dolpo circuit, continuing over the Numa La and Baga La to Phoksundo Lake and back to Juphal, takes about 12–14 days.

faqs.q: Is the Tarap Khola gorge trail dangerous?
faqs.a: It is a rough trail with narrow sections cut into the cliffs, log bridges and occasional rockfall, but it is used regularly by villagers and mule trains. With a good guide, care on exposed sections and no rushing, it is manageable for experienced trekkers. Floods and landslides can damage it; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Are there lodges on the way to Dho Tarap?
faqs.a: There are very few lodges, and they are basic. Most treks to Dho Tarap camp, with tents, a cook and porters or mules. Some villages, such as Dunai and Tarakot, have simple guesthouses. A fully supported camping trek is the reliable choice for Lower Dolpo, especially over the passes.

experiences.title: Over the Numa La and Baga La to Phoksundo
experiences.summary: The great crossing of Lower Dolpo: from Dho Tarap over the Numa La and the Baga La, both above 5,000 m, through high pastures and herders' camps, with wide views of Dhaulagiri and the ranges of Dolpo, down to the turquoise water of Phoksundo Lake.
body: After two nights at Dho Tarap for acclimatisation, we set off west, climbing through grazing land to a high camp below the Numa La. The pass, above 5,000 m, is reached early the next morning after a long, steady climb. From the top, on a clear day, the view runs across range after range of Dolpo and south to the Dhaulagiri massif. Prayer flags and cairns mark the crossing. Take photographs, then keep moving; the wind is cold.

The descent leads into a high valley of pastures and herders' camps, where we camp before the second pass, the Baga La, also above 5,000 m. The days are long, 6–8 hours, and the altitude makes every step count. Weather can change fast, with snow possible even in autumn, so the crew carries everything needed for a forced extra night. Camps here are cold, often well below freezing at night, so a good sleeping bag and dry layers matter.

Beyond the Baga La the trail drops through birch and juniper towards the Suligad valley, and finally to Ringmo and Phoksundo Lake, a welcome sight after the passes. This crossing is for fit, experienced trekkers with good acclimatisation and a strong support crew. Allow at least one spare day for weather, and check current conditions on the passes before you travel. It is a fitting end to the circuit, and a hot meal waits in Ringmo.

faqs.q: How high are the Numa La and Baga La?
faqs.a: Both passes are above 5,000 m; published figures vary between sources, with the Numa La usually given as the higher of the two. They are the highest points of the Lower Dolpo circuit. Neither is technical in good conditions, but altitude, long days and possible snow make them serious undertakings for well-acclimatised trekkers.

faqs.q: Can beginners cross the passes from Dho Tarap to Phoksundo?
faqs.a: We do not recommend it for first-time trekkers. The crossing involves long days above 4,500 m, two passes over 5,000 m and very remote country with no rescue nearby. Previous high-altitude trekking experience, good fitness and a strong support crew are essential. Shorter Lower Dolpo options exist.

faqs.q: What if it snows on the Numa La?
faqs.a: Snow is possible even in autumn. A good crew carries enough food and fuel for extra nights, and the guide will wait, turn back or choose an alternative if conditions are unsafe. Build at least one spare day into your itinerary, and do not push on in poor visibility or deep snow.

experiences.title: A day with the farming nomads of Tarap
experiences.summary: Spend a day with families in Dho Tarap, in the fields at harvest or with herders on the high pastures, to see samadrok, the 'farming nomad' life that combines barley at 4,000 m with yak herding and long-distance trade.
body: Farming in Dho Tarap happens at the very edge of what is possible. In summer, barley, buckwheat and a few vegetables grow in walled fields watered by channels from the streams. At harvest, usually in September, whole families work together cutting, carrying and threshing, often singing as they go. With your guide, you can join a family for a morning in the fields, learn how the crops are cut and stacked, and share a meal.

Higher up, on pastures at 4,000–5,000 m, herders keep yaks, dri, sheep and goats through the summer months, living in tents or stone huts. Visiting a herding camp means a walk of an hour or more above the village. You see milking, butter-churning and cheese-making, and drink salty butter tea by the fire. Herders may talk about grazing, wolves, snow leopards and the weather. Wear warm layers; the pastures are cold and windy.

Your guide explains how samadrok, this mix of fields and herding, along with trade, has kept people alive in Dolpo for centuries, and how it is changing with roads, schools and migration. Be patient and respectful: this is people's working day, not a performance. Offer a small payment or gift for meals, and always ask before taking photographs of people or animals. It is a day you will not forget.

faqs.q: What does samadrok mean?
faqs.a: Samadrok is a Tibetan term used for the way of life in Dolpo, roughly 'farming nomads'. Families grow barley and other crops in walled fields near the villages and move their yaks, sheep and goats between the villages and high pastures at 4,000–5,000 m. Trade with Tibet and the lower hills has traditionally completed the picture.

faqs.q: When is harvest in Dho Tarap?
faqs.a: Barley and buckwheat in Dho Tarap are usually harvested in September, depending on the year's weather. It is a busy time, with whole families in the fields. Summer, from July to August, is when herders are on the high pastures. Both are good times to see daily life, though the monsoon can disrupt flights to Juphal.

faqs.q: Can I stay with a family in Dho Tarap?
faqs.a: A few families offer simple homestay rooms, and on organised camping treks we can arrange meals or tea in family kitchens. Facilities are very basic: shared toilets, no showers and cold rooms. It is a rare chance to see Dolpo life closely. Book through your trekking company and bring your own sleeping bag.

faqs.q: Where is Dho Tarap?
faqs.a: Dho Tarap is in the Tarap valley of Lower Dolpo, in Dolpa district, Karnali Province, at about 4,040 m. It is part of Dolpo Buddha rural municipality. Dho Tarap is about 5–6 days' trek from Juphal airport, or 3–4 days from Phoksundo Lake over the Numa La and Baga La passes.

faqs.q: What permits do I need for Dho Tarap?
faqs.a: Dho Tarap is in Lower Dolpo, a restricted area. As we understand it, you need a Lower Dolpo restricted area permit, around USD 20 per person per week, a Shey Phoksundo National Park permit if you continue to the lake, and a licensed guide, arranged by a registered agency for at least two trekkers. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How long is the Lower Dolpo trek with Dho Tarap?
faqs.a: The Lower Dolpo circuit, from Juphal via the Tarap Khola to Dho Tarap, over the Numa La and Baga La to Phoksundo Lake, and back to Juphal, usually takes 12–14 days of trekking, plus flights to and from Nepalgunj. Allow 16–18 days from Kathmandu, including spare days for weather.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Dho Tarap?
faqs.a: May–June and September–October are best, with stable weather on the passes and clearer skies. July and August are possible in Dolpo's partial rain shadow, but flights to Juphal are often disrupted. From November to April, snow closes the passes and many families move to lower villages.

faqs.q: How difficult is the trek to Dho Tarap?
faqs.a: It is challenging. Days are 5–8 hours on rough, remote trails, the gorge has exposed sections and the passes beyond Dho Tarap exceed 5,000 m. There are few lodges, so most treks camp. You need good fitness, previous trekking experience and time to acclimatise, plus a strong support crew.

faqs.q: Are there lodges in Dho Tarap?
faqs.a: There are a few very basic lodges and homestays, but most organised treks camp. Facilities are simple: shared toilets, no showers and cold rooms. A fully supported camping trek with a cook and porters or mules is the reliable choice, especially if you plan to cross the passes to Phoksundo.

faqs.q: Who are the people of Dho Tarap?
faqs.a: The people of Dho Tarap are Dolpo-pa, who speak a dialect of Tibetan and Nepali and follow Bon and Tibetan Buddhism. They farm barley and buckwheat, herd yaks, sheep and goats on high pastures and trade with Tibet and the lower hills. Around 900 people lived in Dho Tarap at the 2011 census.

faqs.q: Is altitude sickness a risk at Dho Tarap?
faqs.a: Yes. Dho Tarap is at about 4,040 m and the passes beyond exceed 5,000 m. The slow approach from Juphal helps, but you should spend at least two nights in the valley before crossing the passes, drink plenty of water and descend if symptoms worsen. Rescue is slow and weather-dependent.

faqs.q: Can I combine Dho Tarap with Upper Mustang?
faqs.a: Not easily on foot. Dolpo and Mustang are linked by long, high and very remote routes through Upper Dolpo, which need a separate expensive permit and a fully supported expedition. Most travellers visit them on separate trips: Mustang via Jomsom, Dolpo via Nepalgunj and Juphal. Check current status before you travel.
